courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Turning a script into a command-line tool with argparse
question: authscan exits with code 2 when the log file is missing. A teammate suggests returning 0 instead, "since no alerts were found". Why is that a bad idea?
options: Exit code 0 is reserved for Windows
A scheduler would read 0 as a clean run, so a deleted or rotated log would look exactly like a quiet night
argparse will crash if main returns 0
It makes the JSON output invalid
explain: Exit codes are the contract with automation. "Could not check" must never look like "checked, nothing found", especially since attackers delete logs. Keep the error distinct and loud.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
question: Your merchandising team edits the synonym list every week and it includes rules like `tv, television, flat screen`. Which setup fits?
options: synonym filter in the index analyzer, reindex weekly
synonym filter at both index and search time so scores stay consistent
Expand synonyms in application code by duplicating every document
synonym_graph in the search analyzer, backed by a synonym set or an updateable file
explain: Search time lets the list change without reindexing, and synonym_graph is the filter that handles the multi-word entry flat screen correctly. The index-time synonym filter cannot store multi-position tokens faithfully.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
question: Your chat RAG app concatenates the last five turns into the retrieval query. Users report that after they switch topic, answers keep citing documents about the old topic. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the number of retrieved passages so the new topic also appears
Rewrite the latest turn into a standalone query using the history, and retrieve with that alone
Concatenate only the last two turns instead of five
Embed each turn separately and average the vectors
explain: Concatenation (with any window) and averaging both keep old-topic words in the query. A rewriter reads the history to resolve references but outputs only what the current turn needs, so a topic switch produces a query about the new topic.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
question: With the default model (TTFT 0.3 s, 100 tokens/s), you can either run 3 independent sub-queries generated by one call, or a 3-hop Self-Ask chain. Why is the chain slower?
options: The chain retrieves more documents
Each hop needs the previous hop's answer, so its LLM calls (each paying TTFT) run one after another instead of being merged into one call
Self-Ask uses a larger model by definition
Parallel queries skip the reader
explain: Independent sub-queries come out of a single generation call and are searched in parallel, so the critical path has one extra call. A chain has one call per hop on the critical path, and every call pays TTFT plus decoding again.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: The unbiased estimator and its O(1/sqrt(D)) error
question: A colleague estimates inner products with <o-bar,q> directly, skipping the division. What happens to a ranking of documents for one query?
options: Nothing; the ranking is identical because every estimate is scaled by exactly the same constant
Estimates become unbiased but noisier
Each document's estimate is scaled by its own <o-bar,o>, which varies per vector, so the ranking gets extra noise and the distances are biased
The code must be recomputed
explain: The scaling factor is not a global constant: it is about 0.8 on average but differs from vector to vector, because it depends on how evenly each rotated vector spreads its length. The paper also notes this direct estimator is provably biased, which matters when plugged into equation (2) for distances.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Discounts, refunds and rewards: value that can be claimed twice
question: A shop adds loyalty points when an order is placed and never removes them when the order is cancelled. What is the correct fix?
options: Add a CAPTCHA to the cancel button
Show the points balance only after delivery
Limit each account to five cancellations a month
Grant points only when payment settles, and reverse them if the order is cancelled or refunded
explain: The flaw is granting value before the action is final. Tying the grant to settlement, and reversing it on cancellation, keeps points equal to what was really bought. A cancellation limit only slows the abuse; hiding the balance changes nothing.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Starbucks gift cards and two browser sessions (2015)
question: Starbucks cleared the session after each confirmed transfer. Why did that not stop Homakov's race?
options: Because the session cookie was not marked HttpOnly
Because the race used two different sessions of the same account, and the balance being spent is shared across sessions
Because the confirmation used GET instead of POST
Because gift card numbers were guessable
explain: Clearing session 1 only affects session 1. The card balance lives in the database and is reachable from every session of the account, so two sessions can each run one confirmation at the same moment. The control protected the path, not the resource.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Why "too fast to exploit" fails: jitter and the single-packet attack
question: Why does putting the final frames of 20 HTTP/2 requests into one TCP packet defeat network jitter?
options: Because HTTP/2 encrypts the frames
Because TCP packets travel faster than HTTP/1.1 packets
Because a single packet arrives as a unit, so all 20 requests become complete at the same instant regardless of the path's delay variation
Because the server processes HTTP/2 requests in a single thread
explain: Jitter changes when each packet arrives. If the bytes that complete every request are in one packet, they all arrive together, so the server sees 20 complete requests at once. Encryption and speed are irrelevant, and HTTP/2 servers still process streams concurrently.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
question: You run a 3-server cluster and add a fourth server for extra safety. How many simultaneous server failures can the cluster now survive while staying available?
options: 1, the same as before
2, one more than before
3, since one server is enough to serve reads
0, because 4 cannot form a majority
explain: With n = 4 the majority is 3, so only 1 server may be down. You added replication cost (one more copy on every write) without improving availability. Go to 5 servers to tolerate 2 failures.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
question: A team switches to lease-based reads to cut read latency. Under which condition can a client now see stale data?
options: When a follower's disk is slow
When the old leader's clock runs slow, so it keeps serving reads after a new leader has been elected
When two clients read the same key at once
Never; leases are as safe as ReadIndex
explain: A lease assumes the leader's sense of elapsed time matches the followers'. If its clock is slow or the process pauses, it may believe the lease is still valid after followers have timed out and elected someone else, and serve stale data. ReadIndex avoids this by checking with a majority on every batch of reads.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
question: A statement cites [2][5]. Passage [5] alone entails it; [2] alone does not, and [5] without [2] still entails it. How does ALCE score this?
options: Citation recall 1; citation [2] counts as irrelevant, lowering precision
Citation recall 0, because [2] does not support the statement
Citation recall 1 and precision 1, since the statement is supported
Citation recall 0.5, one supporting passage out of two
explain: Recall asks whether the concatenation of cited passages entails the statement: yes, thanks to [5]. Precision checks each citation: [2] neither supports alone nor is needed with the others, so it is irrelevant.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
question: Why do LETOR and MSLR compute BM25 separately on body, anchor, title and URL instead of once on the whole page?
options: A match in the title and a match in the body are different evidence, and separate features let the model learn a weight for each
BM25 cannot be computed on long documents
It makes the index smaller
Search engines are required to by the TREC rules
explain: Per-field (per-stream) scores keep the evidence separate. A model can then learn that a title match is worth more than a body match for this collection, which a single whole-document score cannot express.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
question: A team logs only document ids and query strings, then recomputes all features nightly for training. Which feature is most at risk of skew?
options: URL length
Number of query terms
Freshness computed from age relative to now
Whether the title contains a query term
explain: URL length, query term count and title containment are stable for a fixed document and query. Freshness relative to now is recomputed hours or days later, so every training example looks older than it was when the user saw it.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
question: For a first-stage retriever whose top 100 candidates are passed to a cross-encoder reranker (a slower model that reads the query and each candidate together and rescores it), which metric best measures the retriever?
options: RR, since users only look at the first result
nDCG@10 with exponential gain
R@100, the share of relevant documents that make it into the candidate set
explain: The reranker can only reorder what the retriever passes on, so the retriever's job is coverage at depth 100. Order inside the 100 matters little because the reranker rescores them. Top-heavy metrics such as RR, P@1 or nDCG@10 belong to the final ranking.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Trust among thieves: exit scams, takedowns and a fragmented market
question: In March 2024 BlackCat posted a law enforcement seizure notice that researchers said was copied from the FBI's December notice, days after a USD 22 million payment arrived. What was the most likely purpose?
options: To comply with a court order after a second FBI raid
To disappear with the affiliate's share while blaming the police: an exit scam
To warn victims that payments were no longer safe
To raise the affiliate share to 90 percent
explain: Krebs reported the affiliate Notchy complaining that BlackCat kept the payment and suspended their account, and Fabian Wosar of Emsisoft called it an exit scam. The FBI did not claim a new seizure. The affiliate kept the data, which is why trust collapsing among criminals is also a risk for victims.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Change Healthcare and ALPHV, February 2024
question: Which single control would most directly have blocked the initial access Witty described?
options: Immutable backups
A data leak site monitoring service
Faster pharmacy restoration
MFA on the Citrix remote access portal
explain: The entry was a stolen password on a portal that did not require MFA. Backups and monitoring matter for impact and response, but they do not stop the login.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Backups that survive an attacker with Domain Admin
question: Why does the model say VM snapshots on the same ESXi hosts are lost in scenario A?
options: Snapshots are always encrypted by ransomware first
They live on the platform the attacker controls, so the same access that encrypts the VMs deletes the snapshots
Snapshots expire after 24 hours
AD stores the snapshot keys
explain: A copy inside the failure domain shares its fate. Snapshots are useful for quick rollbacks, not as a ransomware recovery copy.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Queue pairs, work requests and the completion queue
question: A program posts receive buffers and sends but never calls `ibv_poll_cq` on a busy CQ. What happens according to the verbs documentation?
options: Old CQEs are silently overwritten and traffic continues
The NIC stops sending until the CQ has room, like TCP flow control
The kernel enlarges the CQ automatically
The CQ overruns: IBV_EVENT_CQ_ERR is raised and the CQ can no longer be used
explain: The ibv_poll_cq man page warns that you must consume completions fast enough to avoid overrun; an overrun triggers IBV_EVENT_CQ_ERR and the CQ becomes unusable, and the manual adds that its QPs get a fatal event. Size the CQ for the maximum number of outstanding signaled WRs and receives.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
question: Why does RoCEv2 put a UDP header in front of the IB transport header?
options: UDP provides retransmission for RDMA
UDP is required for PFC to work
To make RoCEv2 compatible with iWARP
So routers and switches can hash flows across equal-cost paths (ECMP); IP provides routing
explain: The DCQCN paper: the IP header is needed for routing, while the UDP header is needed for ECMP. Reliability still comes from the IB transport in the NIC, not from UDP.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
question: A client sends "my position is (20, 10)" every frame and the server copies it into the world. What is the core problem?
options: It uses too much bandwidth
The server cannot interpolate it
WebSocket frames cannot carry positions
The client is authoritative over its own position, so a modified client can teleport or move through walls
explain: Trusting client-reported state defeats the authoritative design. The client should send intents (move right) and the server should compute the resulting position and reject impossible moves.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
question: With plain cosine and blanks as 0, Space1 and Rom1 come out at +0.28 although fans of one rate the other 1 star. Why?
options: Cosine is undefined for rating data, so the value is noise
All ratings are positive, so any two items rated by the same users share direction; adjusted cosine removes each user's mean first
The users who rated both items gave them identical ratings
Rom1 has more ratings than Space1, which inflates the cosine
explain: With non-negative entries the cosine can never be negative. Subtracting each user's average rating (adjusted cosine) turns 'rated 1 by a sci-fi fan' into a negative number, and the similarity becomes -0.97.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
question: In LinUCB, an arm has never been shown. What is its score p for any context x?
options: 0, so it is never chosen until an exploration phase
alpha times the norm of x, since A is the identity and b is zero, so it is likely to be tried
Its popularity
Undefined until the arm gets one reward
explain: With A_a = I and b_a = 0, theta is 0 and the bonus is alpha times the square root of x transpose x, the length of x. Unseen arms therefore carry the largest uncertainty bonus, which is how LinUCB explores new items.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: How wrong is it? Corner noise, out-of-plane height, pixels
question: Your measured lengths have about 1 mm of scatter between photos. Which change most directly reduces corner-noise error?
options: Switch from a homography to the pixels-per-mm ratio
Print a larger marker and place the object within or close to its footprint
Increase JPEG compression to reduce noise
Use a marker dictionary with more IDs
explain: A 1 px corner error is a smaller fraction of a larger marker, and objects inside the reference footprint are interpolated, not extrapolated (0.24 mm versus 1.28 mm in the toy). Dictionary size affects ID confusion, not corner accuracy.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
question: A query joins 14 tables listed in FROM with default settings. How does PostgreSQL search for a join order?
options: With the Genetic Query Optimizer, since 14 is at least geqo_threshold (12)
Exhaustive dynamic programming over all 14 tables
It joins them in the order written
It refuses to plan queries over 12 tables
explain: GEQO is used for queries with at least geqo_threshold FROM items, 12 by default. It finds a reasonable order quickly but not necessarily the best. Exhaustive search would cost too much planning time at this size.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
question: Why does Dynamo accept the risk that a sloppy quorum's read and write sets may not overlap?
options: Because vector clocks make overlap unnecessary
Because it prefers accepting writes (an always-writeable cart) and reconciles divergent versions later
Because $R + W > N$ still holds, so overlap is guaranteed anyway
Because hinted replicas are counted twice
explain: Dynamo is designed to be always writeable: rejecting an add-to-cart is worse than briefly reading an old cart. It pays for that with possible divergence, which it detects with vector clocks and resolves at read time. That is the next lesson.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: What RLHF reward hacking looks like: length, sycophancy, persuasion
question: After PPO your reward rose by 0.9. Sorting outputs into 20-token length buckets, the average reward within each bucket rose by only 0.05. What does this most likely mean?
options: The reward model is well calibrated
The KL penalty was too strong
Most of the gain came from moving outputs into longer buckets: the policy mainly learned to be longer
Quality improved, but the buckets are too wide to show it
explain: This is Singhal et al.'s non-length reward gain: within-bucket improvement is small, so the total gain is explained by the shift toward longer outputs. A length-only reward would likely recover much of the same improvement. Narrower buckets would not create within-bucket gains that are not there.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
question: In a GRPO group, all 4 rollouts use the same hack and all get reward 1. What is the advantage of each, and what does that imply?
options: 0 each (zero variance), so this group adds no gradient; the hack was already reinforced when it competed with honest failures
+1 each, so the hack is reinforced as strongly as ever
-1 each, so GRPO automatically corrects saturated hacks
Undefined, so training crashes
explain: All rewards equal the mean, so every advantage is 0 (implementations add a small epsilon to the standard deviation to avoid dividing by zero). Saturated groups stop teaching anything, including how to solve the task honestly. The damage happened earlier, in mixed groups where the hack stood out.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
question: Two risks score 20 on a 5 x 5 grid: (likelihood 5, impact 4) and (likelihood 4, impact 5). What does that tell you about their expected yearly loss?
options: They are equal
Nothing reliable: the scores are ranks, so you need money estimates to compare them
The first is always larger
The second is always larger
explain: Ordinal levels do not carry magnitudes. Impact 5 might mean ten times impact 4, or twice. Equal grid scores can hide very different expected losses.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
question: Which CSF 2.0 Function contains the subcategory 'Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated, and maintained'?
options: Govern
Identify
Protect
Recover
explain: It is GV.RM-02, in the Risk Management Strategy category of Govern. Appetite is a governance decision, which is why 2.0 moved such outcomes into the new function.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: One control, many frameworks: CIS Controls, HIPAA and the crosswalk
question: Your company must meet both HIPAA (encryption at rest addressable) and PCI DSS (PAN unreadable wherever stored). How should the encryption control be designed?
options: One control built to the stricter requirement, mapped to both, with one set of evidence
Two separate controls with separate evidence
Skip it for HIPAA because addressable means optional
Only encrypt the card data and document nothing else
explain: Building once to the strictest requirement and mapping it is the point of a crosswalk. Addressable is not optional: not implementing needs a documented reason and an equivalent alternative.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Third-party risk: questionnaires, SBOMs and concentration risk
question: A tier 1 vendor's SOC 2 Type II period ended nine months ago. What is the most reasonable request?
options: A bridge letter covering the gap, then the next report when issued, and a check of exceptions and complementary user entity controls
Nothing; Type II reports are valid forever
A Type I report instead
Their ISO 9001 certificate
explain: Reports cover a past period. A bridge letter is the vendor's statement about the gap. Exceptions and CUECs tell you what the report does not cover.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
question: A team switches its GRPO run from a 4k to a 32k maximum response length. Training time per token is unchanged. Which stage's share of the step most likely grows?
options: Rollout, because decode steps are sequential and the batch waits for its longest response
The optimizer step, because more tokens produce larger gradients
Reference logprobs, because the reference model is frozen
Weight sync, because longer responses need more weight bytes
explain: Rollout grows most: each extra token is one more sequential decode step, and a synchronous batch waits for its longest member. The optimizer step and weight sync do not depend on response length, and the logprob passes are parallel over tokens.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
question: NeMo RL async GRPO runs with max_trajectory_age_steps: 1. A trajectory was generated with weights v10. At which training steps can it be used?
options: Steps 10 and 11; at step 12 it is discarded
Only step 10
Steps 9, 10 and 11
Any step, as long as importance sampling correction is on
explain: The docs' own example: a trajectory generated with v10 can be used for training steps v10 or v11, and at step v12 it is too old and is discarded. Importance correction handles the remaining mismatch; it does not remove the age limit.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
question: Your Alertmanager groups by alert name only, not by service. During this incident the group named ServiceLatencyHigh contains alerts from checkout, pricing, catalog and cart. What have you lost?
options: Nothing: grouping is lossless, and the labels are still in the notification
The error-ratio alerts, because grouping keeps only one alert type per group
The ability to see at a glance which services are affected and which are not, because one group now hides the per-service pattern that points at the cause
The SLO burn alert, which is always inhibited by instance-level alerts
explain: Grouping is lossless in principle (the labels travel with the group), but the grouping key decides what the notification shows you first. Grouping by name alone merges unrelated services into one blob and destroys exactly the signal you want: which parts of the graph are anomalous. Group by something that preserves topology, such as alert name plus service or cluster.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
question: At 20:22 you are 90 percent sure catalog's pool config is the cause but you do not know how the value 4 got rendered. What do you do?
options: Keep digging until you understand the rendering, so the revert cannot make things worse
Revert the config now, confirm the symptom clears, and work out how the value got rendered afterwards
Raise the pool to 128 to add margin, since you are unsure of the right value
Wait for the config owner to wake up, since they can explain the render
explain: Reverting to a state the system ran in minutes ago is the lowest-risk action available, and the recovery is itself evidence for your hypothesis. Understanding the template can happen with users served. Raising the pool to 128 sounds prudent but changes to an untested value, and waiting for the config owner extends a user-visible outage for a conversation.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Weighted RRF and multi-query fusion (RAG-Fusion)
question: Why does a single off-topic rewrite in RAG-Fusion usually do limited damage to the fused list?
options: RRF uses the cosine scores, which are lower for off-topic results
The LLM answer step re-sorts documents by relevance
Its documents get at most one vote of about 1/61, while documents shared by several rewrites collect several votes
RRF detects off-topic queries and drops them
explain: RRF knows nothing about topicality. The protection is structural: a document returned by only one of four lists can reach about 1/61, while documents several lists agree on get two to four votes. The same mechanism also buries a uniquely good rewrite's finds.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
question: In C, a driver function takes a spinlock, calls a helper that returns an error, and returns early without unlocking. Which part of the Rust version prevents the equivalent bug?
options: The borrow checker forbids early returns while a lock is held
lockdep runs at compile time in Rust
The guard returned by `lock()` is dropped on every exit path, and its `Drop` calls the backend's unlock
Rust spinlocks are released automatically by the scheduler
explain: Early returns are allowed; they simply run destructors for live locals. `Guard::drop` calls `B::unlock`. lockdep still runs at runtime as in C; the Guard constructor even asserts the lock is held.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
question: The sample's ioctl returns `Err(ENOTTY)` for an unknown command. What does the userspace `ioctl()` call return?
options: 0, because the Rust error is swallowed by the trampoline
-25 directly as the return value
-1, with errno set to 25 (ENOTTY)
The process receives SIGSEGV
explain: `ENOTTY` is 25. The trampoline returns `err.to_errno()` = -25 to the VFS (virtual file system, the layer that dispatched the call to the driver). The system call returns -25 to the C library, which stores 25 in `errno` and returns -1. The userspace test in the sample prints this with `perror`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
question: Two CPU-bound tasks at the same nice share one CPU under EEVDF. X requests a 0.5 ms slice, Y requests 4 ms. What share does X get in the long run?
options: About 89 percent, since 4 / (4 + 0.5) of the deadlines favor X
About 11 percent, since X asks for so little each time
About 50 percent: equal weights, X just runs in shorter, more frequent pieces
It depends on HZ, because slices end on ticks
explain: Share follows weight. Eligibility ($v_i \le V$) stops X from running ahead of the average however early its deadlines are. The short request only makes X run sooner and in smaller pieces.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
question: Your loader opened and loaded the skeleton without errors, but /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state still says disabled. Which step is missing?
options: The verifier has not run yet
Creating DSQ 0
Attaching the struct_ops map (SCX_OPS_ATTACH, bpf_map__attach_struct_ops)
Setting a nice value on the loader
explain: Loading only verifies and loads programs and maps. The scheduler becomes active when the struct_ops map is attached as a link; ops.init(), which creates DSQ 0, runs as part of that registration.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production
question: A scheduler with the default timeout has a bug: tasks of one cgroup are inserted into a custom DSQ that dispatch never reads. What do you observe?
options: Those tasks freeze, then within about 30 to 45 s the scheduler is unloaded with a stall error and everything runs on fair again
The machine hangs until rebooted because BPF code runs with interrupts disabled
The verifier refuses to load the scheduler because a DSQ is never consumed
The tasks run anyway because custom DSQs fall back to the global DSQ after one slice
explain: The verifier checks memory safety and termination, not whether your policy eventually runs every task. The watchdog sees runnable tasks older than 30 s on its next check (every 15 s), exits with SCX_EXIT_ERROR_STALL, and tasks revert to the fair class.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: How secret scanners find keys: patterns, entropy, verification
question: In the toy scanner, `password = "changeme123"` was skipped. What does that show?
options: Entropy thresholds trade false positives for false negatives: weak human passwords score low and can be missed
The regular expression is wrong
changeme123 is not a secret
Shannon entropy only works on hexadecimal
explain: The pattern matched; the entropy filter rejected the value because human-chosen passwords are not random. That filter is what keeps scanners usable on large codebases, at the price of missing exactly the weakest passwords.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Dynamic secrets and leases: credentials that expire on their own
question: An attacker copies a dynamic credential from an app's debug log. The app keeps renewing the lease every 50 minutes (TTL 1 h, max TTL 24 h). How long can the attacker use the copy?
options: At most 1 hour
Forever, because renewal resets the maximum
Not at all, because dynamic credentials are bound to the app's IP address
Until the lease reaches its 24-hour maximum or someone revokes it, because the app's renewals keep the same credential alive
explain: Renewal extends the same username and password, so the attacker benefits from it. The max TTL is the hard stop. Dynamic database credentials are not bound to a network address unless the database itself enforces that, so revoke the lease as soon as misuse is seen.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key ceremonies: the DNS root key and multi-person control
question: Which control in the root KSK design stops the same small group from both activating the HSM and restoring its keys elsewhere?
options: Separate roles with separate quorums: Crypto Officers activate, Recovery Key Share Holders restore
Tamper-evident bags
Quarterly ceremonies
FIPS level 3 HSMs
explain: Separation of duties: the people who can switch the key on are not the people who can rebuild it, so an attacker must corrupt both groups. The other controls protect the hardware and the schedule.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Taint by hand: following one value from source to sink
question: Which of these is a correct sanitizer for a value that will become part of a SQL query string?
options: `html.escape(value)`
`value.strip()`
`int(value)`, used only where a number is expected
`value.replace("'", "")`
explain: int() can only return a number, which cannot contain SQL syntax, so its output is safe for that sink. html.escape targets HTML, strip() removes only whitespace, and deleting quotes is a blocklist that breaks names like O'Brien and misses injection that needs no quote. Parameterised queries remain the better fix.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Regular expressions that hang: ReDoS and the Cloudflare outage
question: Which pattern is the ReDoS risk when matched against long user input in JavaScript?
options: `^https://example\.com/`
explain: `(\d+)+` nests one quantifier inside another, so a long run of digits followed by a non-digit has exponentially many ways to fail. The others have bounded or unambiguous structure: each character can be matched in only one way.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Apple goto fail: one duplicated line in C
question: Which single defence would most reliably have caught goto fail before release, according to the sources in this lesson?
options: A longer code freeze before each iOS release
Renaming the label from fail to cleanup
A negative test that connects to a server whose handshake is signed with the wrong key
Running the code under AddressSanitizer
explain: A test that must fail (bad signature) would have passed instead, exposing the bug immediately; Langley built exactly such a test server. AddressSanitizer finds memory errors, and this was a logic error with no bad memory access. Renaming and code freezes change nothing.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: what safe Rust promises, and reviewing unsafe
question: The CVE-2021-31162 proof of concept contained `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. What does that show?
options: The attribute does not work
Rust has no memory safety guarantees
Undefined behaviour can come from unsafe code in libraries you call, including std, not just your own
Panics are always memory errors
explain: forbid(unsafe_code) guaranteed the program itself had no unsafe blocks; the double free was inside the standard library's own unsafe implementation of Vec::from_iter. The guarantee covers your code, and relies on the soundness of everything beneath it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
question: You found SQL injection in an internal admin-only report page that runs with a read-only database account. How should severity be described?
options: Critical: SQL injection is always critical
Informational: admins can be trusted
Reachable only by admins and limited to reads by the account's permissions: lower than the same bug on a public page, but still a real finding to fix
Not a finding, because the account is read-only
explain: Severity combines impact and reachability. Admin-only access and a read-only account both reduce it, but a compromised admin session or a malicious insider could still read data they should not. Say exactly that, and recommend parameterisation anyway.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IKEv2: four messages to build the keys and the first tunnel
question: At which point can both IKEv2 peers compute the encryption keys for the IKE SA?
options: After message 2, once both Diffie-Hellman values and nonces have been exchanged
After message 4, once both AUTH payloads have been verified
Before message 1, from the pre-shared key alone
Only after the first ESP packet arrives
explain: SKEYSEED depends on the Diffie-Hellman secret and both nonces, all known after IKE_SA_INIT. That is why messages 3 and 4 can already be encrypted. Authentication comes later, in IKE_AUTH.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SSH's transport layer: version, KEXINIT, key exchange and host keys
question: In OpenSSH 10.3's debug output, what does "kex: algorithm: mlkem768x25519-sha256" tell an auditor?
options: The session uses a hybrid of ML-KEM-768 and X25519 for key agreement, so recorded traffic resists a future quantum computer
The host key is a post-quantum signature key
The connection uses no Diffie-Hellman at all
The MAC algorithm is SHA-256 based on ML-KEM
explain: The kex line names the key agreement method only. Host keys are reported separately (here ssh-ed25519, still classical). The hybrid includes X25519 Diffie-Hellman alongside ML-KEM.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SNMPv3: managing devices without a password in every packet
question: An auditor finds SNMPv3 configured at the authNoPriv level. What does that protect, and what does it not?
options: It encrypts the data but does not authenticate the sender
It authenticates messages and blocks replays, but the values (configurations, counters) travel unencrypted
It provides no protection; it is the same as SNMPv2c
It protects everything, because authentication implies encryption
explain: authNoPriv adds an HMAC and the timeliness check, so forged and replayed messages are rejected, but there is no privacy: anyone on the path can read the payload. authPriv adds encryption.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Choosing and auditing secure protocols, and the post-quantum plan
question: A company runs a strong IKEv2 configuration with certificates, but its VPN gateway's web login page has an unpatched authentication bypass. Which statement is right?
options: The gateway is at risk: an internet-facing appliance can be compromised through its software, whatever protocol it speaks
The VPN is safe because the IPsec cryptography is strong
Only users who log in through the web page are at risk
IKEv2 encrypts the web login page, so the bug cannot be reached
explain: The protocol and the product are separate. Attackers have repeatedly taken over VPN appliances through bugs in their web components, then harvested credentials and moved inward. Patch and monitor the appliance itself.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions and separation of duty
question: A developer runs a one-off UPDATE in the production accounts table to fix a customer's balance, without going through the application. Which Clark-Wilson rule does this break most directly?
options: C1: IVPs must validate CDIs
E3: users must be authenticated
C5: UDIs must be validated
E1: only certified TPs may change CDIs
explain: The developer changed a CDI without any certified TP. They were probably authenticated (E3 holds), the IVP may even pass by luck (C1), and no UDI was turned into a CDI by a TP (C5 is about TPs).

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
question: Google's migration put a user on enforcement only after over 99.99% of their traffic had been eligible for 30 days in logging mode. What problem does that rule solve?
options: It avoids breaking real work by enforcing before all of a user's workflows function through the new path
It prevents attackers from guessing the rules
It reduces bandwidth costs
It satisfies a legal requirement for 30 days of logs
explain: Logging mode shows exactly which traffic would be dropped. Waiting for near-complete eligibility means enforcement breaks almost nothing, and the leftover flows point to workflows that still need fixing or an exemption.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
question: Which design most limits the damage if the remote-access component at the edge is fully compromised?
options: A bigger VPN appliance with more CPU
A VPN that gives remote users the whole internal network, plus a strong perimeter firewall
Per-application access where each application verifies a signed, audience-bound identity assertion and users authenticate with phishing-resistant MFA at a separate identity provider
Hiding the VPN's address from public DNS
explain: Per-application access limits reach; app-side verification means a foothold at the edge is not trusted by default; phishing-resistant MFA at a separate identity provider means a hijacked edge page does not yield reusable passwords. Hiding the address is security by obscurity, and internet-wide scans find it anyway.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Running a security design review
question: Which finding is written so that an engineer can act on it?
options: "The design violates zero trust."
"Least privilege is not followed."
"The reporting role has UPDATE on invoices (grant in db/roles.sql line 14); move reporting to a read-only replica; owner data-team; before Q1."
"Consider improving database security."
explain: It states the risk in system terms, gives checkable evidence, recommends a specific change, and assigns an owner and a deadline. The others name principles or vague goals without saying what to change.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Idempotent steps: designing work that is safe to run twice
question: Which step is NOT idempotent as written?
options: Set case tag 'vpn-spray'
Disable account j.doe
Look up 203.0.113.7 in the intel cache
Append 'enrichment done' to the case notes
explain: Each append adds another note, so running it twice leaves two notes. Setting a tag and disabling an account reach the same state however often they run, and a lookup changes nothing.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLM-assisted triage: the model advises, code and people decide
question: The model replies {suggestion: likely_benign, evidence: [{field: src.owner, value: corporate scanner}]}, but the alert has no src.owner field. What should the pipeline do?
options: Accept it: the model may know the scanner from its training data
Add a src.owner field to the alert so the evidence matches
Close the alert, since evidence was provided
Reject the reply, log it as a confabulation, and leave the alert with the analyst without AI advice
explain: Evidence that is not in the alert is invented, whatever the model's confidence. Editing the alert to fit the model corrupts the record, and closing on a rejected reply is the outcome the check exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: When not to automate, and a design review checklist
question: Which step fits 'robot prepares, human approves'?
options: Adding asset and identity context to every new alert
Opening a case for each new alert
Sending the company-wide breach notification email
Isolating one employee laptop from the network after a confirmed malicious download
explain: Isolation disrupts one person and is awkward to undo, so a quick human check is worth it, but the blast radius is one machine and speed matters. Enrichment and case creation are safe to automate fully; a company-wide breach notice is a human decision from start to finish.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
question: A company's main worry is ransomware affiliates. Which control best reduces that specific threat?
options: A bigger firewall rule set for outbound web traffic only
Hiding the company's logo from its website
Encrypting the data at rest on servers
Offline backups plus removing unused remote-access accounts
explain: Affiliates commonly enter through exposed remote access with stolen credentials and profit by making data unavailable. Removing unused access shrinks their entry points, and offline backups (which CISA's DarkSide advisory recommends) remove the leverage. Encryption at rest does not stop ransomware from encrypting the data again.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Equifax 2017: a known bug and a missed patch
question: Struts 2.5.10 is installed. Is it vulnerable to CVE-2017-5638?
options: No: 2.5.10 is newer than 2.3.32
No: only 2.3.x was affected
It depends on the CVSS score
Yes: on the 2.5 branch the first fixed version is 2.5.10.1
explain: NVD lists 2.5.x before 2.5.10.1 as affected. Comparing across branches (2.5.10 against 2.3.32) is the classic mistake; compare within the branch.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
question: Under the Supreme Court's reading in Van Buren, which act most clearly 'exceeds authorized access'?
options: An employee reads a report they are allowed to read, for a personal reason
A user forgets to log out
A researcher reads a public security.txt file
A logged-in user changes an ID in a URL to open another customer's records that are off-limits to them
explain: The Court tied 'exceeds authorized access' to entering areas of a computer, such as files or databases, that are off-limits to you. Reading another customer's records fits; misusing data you may see is the case the Court excluded.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Severity you can defend: scores, context and confidence
question: You see an old version banner on a Linux server but did not test the flaw. The vendor is known to backport fixes. How should the finding read?
options: Critical, Confirmed
Omit it entirely
Severity per the scale, Confidence: Possible, with a safe check the owner can run (package changelog or vendor advisory) to confirm or close it
Mark it fixed
explain: A banner is weak evidence when fixes are backported. Stating low confidence and the check that would settle it is honest and saves the owner time.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Incident updates when you do not know yet
question: Why give a fixed time for the next update, even if nothing has changed?
options: Because regulators require it every hour
It makes the incident shorter
It sets expectations, stops people interrupting responders for news, and makes 'no change' itself informative
So the update can be automated
explain: Predictable updates reduce ad hoc questions and let stakeholders plan. Saying 'no change, next update 16:00' is still useful information.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions
question: Under the SEC rules adopted in July 2023, what must a public company describe about the board in its annual report?
options: Each director's password policy
Every vulnerability found during the year
The board's oversight of risks from cybersecurity threats, any responsible committee, and how the board is informed about those risks
Nothing; the rules only cover incidents
explain: Regulation S-K Item 106(c)(1) requires a description of board oversight, the responsible committee if any, and the processes by which the board is informed. Item 1.05 of Form 8-K separately covers material incidents.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
question: Why does ReST-EM cap the number of correct solutions kept per problem?
options: Easy problems produce many more correct samples, so without a cap they would dominate the fine-tuning set
Storage: 64 solutions per problem would not fit in memory
The verifier becomes unreliable after 10 solutions
To keep the dataset exactly the same size every iteration
explain: With 32 samples, a problem solved 90% of the time contributes about 28.8 solutions and one solved 10% of the time about 3.2. The cap of 10 rebalances the data toward harder problems; the paper says it keeps diversity and prevents overfitting to easy problems.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
question: A model is right 90% of the time. Its self-verifier accepts 80% of correct answers and 20% of wrong ones. What is the gap, and what does it say about another round of self-improvement?
options: About 0.07: kept accuracy is 0.973, so the round can add at most about 7 points, minus distillation error
About 0.33, the same as at 30% accuracy, since the verifier did not change
0, because a verifier with 20% false positives can never help
About 0.6, because the verifier is 4 times more likely to accept a right answer
explain: Kept accuracy is 0.72 / (0.72 + 0.02) = 0.973, so the gap is 0.073. The same verifier gave 0.332 at 30% accuracy: as the generator improves there is less left to filter, one reason iterative gains saturate.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Choosing the threshold: hit rate against false hits
question: Which pair is most likely to produce a false hit with a plain embedding similarity threshold?
options: "Do you ship to Canada?" and "Do you ship to Mexico?"
"Do you ship to Canada?" and "Can I get delivery in Canada?"
"How do I reset my password?" and "What is your return policy?"
"What are your opening hours?" and "When are you open?"
explain: Swapping one entity keeps the sentence nearly identical, so the embeddings stay very close while the correct answer changes. The second and fourth pairs are true paraphrases, and the third pair is far apart and will simply miss.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: The server as a confused deputy
question: A PDF export feature renders a user-supplied HTML page on the server, including any images the HTML references. Which confused-deputy risk does this create most directly?
options: Cross-site scripting in the user's browser
The server fetches image URLs the user chose, so it can be pointed at internal hosts (SSRF)
SQL injection in the PDF library
None: PDFs are static files
explain: The renderer fetches every URL the HTML names, from the server's network position. That is SSRF through a feature that does not look like a URL fetcher. OWASP's SSRF cheat sheet gives user-supplied image URLs and webhooks as typical entry points; a document renderer that loads remote images is the same pattern.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Egress filtering, isolation and detecting SSRF
question: Why is an alert on VPC Flow Logs records for 169.254.169.254 not a working detection for metadata SSRF on AWS?
options: Flow logs are encrypted
AWS documents that flow logs do not record traffic to and from the instance metadata address at all
Flow logs only exist for IPv6
The metadata service uses UDP
explain: Metadata traffic never appears in flow logs, so an alert on it can never fire. Use the IMDS CloudWatch metrics, host-level monitoring and credential-use signals (CloudTrail, GuardDuty) instead.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell response: versions, mitigations and detection
question: A server running a vulnerable Log4j sits behind a firewall that denies all outbound connections except to its database. An attacker sends the lookup string. What is the most likely result?
options: Full remote code execution as usual
The lookup triggers an outbound connection attempt that the firewall denies, so the chain breaks and the denied connection shows up in firewall logs
The database is compromised instead
Nothing at all is logged anywhere
explain: The classic chain needs an outbound connection to the attacker's directory server. Default-deny egress breaks it and produces a denial log entry, which is excellent evidence. Patch anyway: lookups that read local data, such as environment variables, can still leak them into logs.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: When front end and back end disagree: smuggling and ProxyLogon
question: In ProxyLogon, why did the back end perform privileged actions for an unauthenticated attacker?
options: The attacker cracked an admin password
Exchange had no back end
The front end forwarded the attacker-routed request using the Exchange server's own Kerberos identity, which the back end trusted
The attacker used request smuggling
explain: The front end lent its own credentials to a request whose destination the attacker chose: SSRF with a confused deputy. The fix validated the routing value as a host name and stopped the front end from authenticating such requests as itself.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Why can't the scheduler simply build batch k+1 while batch k runs, with no extra machinery?
options: Batch k+1 needs batch k's sampled tokens as its inputs, which are not known until batch k finishes; SGLang uses future-token placeholders resolved on the GPU
The GPU cannot run two kernels in a row
Python cannot start a second thread
The radix tree must be rebuilt from scratch every step
explain: For decoding, each step's input is the previous step's output. Overlap therefore needs a way to refer to tokens that do not exist yet. The release notes describe resolving this dependency with future tokens and careful CUDA event synchronization.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
question: To speed things up, someone divides straight-line km by 30 km/h instead of the network's top speed of 60 km/h. What is the risk?
options: None; any distance-based estimate keeps A* optimal
A* will settle more nodes than before
The heuristic may now overestimate on fast roads, so A* can return a slower route than the optimum
The algorithm may loop forever
explain: At 30 km/h each kilometer is estimated at 2 minutes, but a 60 km/h road covers it in 1. Overestimating breaks Theorem 1's condition, so optimality is no longer guaranteed. The survey notes such aggressive bounds speed things up only by giving up correctness.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
question: You record 2 s of data at 1000 Hz and need to tell apart tones at 50.0 Hz and 50.3 Hz. What helps?
options: Zero-pad to 8 times the length before the FFT
Sample at 4000 Hz instead of 1000 Hz for the same 2 s
Record for longer: at least several seconds, since the bin spacing is 1/duration
Apply a Hann window, which sharpens peaks
explain: Resolution is fs/N = 1/duration. Two seconds gives 0.5 Hz bins, too coarse for a 0.3 Hz gap; you need more than 1/0.3 = 3.3 s, and more still with a window, which widens peaks. A higher fs adds bins at high frequencies but keeps the spacing at 1/duration. Zero-padding only interpolates the same blurred spectrum.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
question: You remove the scalar tail loop from sum_avx2 to save code. What happens for n = 19?
options: Nothing, the vector loop reads all 19 elements
It returns 136, silently dropping a[16], a[17] and a[18]
It crashes because the last load is out of bounds
It returns 190 but more slowly
explain: The vector loop stops at i = 16 because 16 + 8 > 19, so it never reads past the end. Without the tail the last 3 elements are never added: you get 136 instead of 190. Silent wrong answers like this are the classic SIMD bug.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: You ship a desktop app built with `-march=x86-64-v4` because benchmarks on your AVX-512 workstation looked great. Users with AVX2-only laptops report crashes at startup. What is the right fix?
options: Add -O3
Build for the baseline or x86-64-v3 and use target_clones or runtime checks for the AVX-512 hot loops
Switch to -ffast-math
Catch SIGILL and retry
explain: x86-64-v4 lets the compiler place AVX-512 instructions anywhere, including startup code. Build the bulk for a level every user has, and multiversion only the hot kernels so each CPU picks its best copy.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
question: A slab holds 31 objects of 128 bytes in a 4096-byte page, with 32 bytes of in-page metadata. Without coloring, every slab's objects start at offset 0. What does coloring change?
options: It fits a 32nd object into the page by moving the metadata elsewhere
It uses the 96 leftover bytes to start each new slab's objects at a different offset, so hot fields of objects in different slabs map to different cache sets
It rounds the objects up to 256 bytes so each one is cache-line aligned
It marks freed objects with a pattern so use-after-free is detected
explain: 31 x 128 = 3968 bytes, plus 32 metadata leaves 96 spare bytes. Coloring spends that otherwise wasted space on an offset that varies per slab. (Filling freed memory with 0xdeadbeef is a separate debugging feature.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
question: You move a working colocated job to separate pools and add `--update-weight-mode delta` but keep the default transport. What happens?
options: It fails an assertion: delta mode requires `--update-weight-transport disk`
It runs, shipping deltas over NCCL
It silently falls back to full NCCL sync
It uses CUDA IPC because the engines are on the same nodes
explain: `create_weight_updater` asserts that delta mode uses disk transport (and is not colocated). Delta sync works by publishing versioned checkpoint directories that engines pull, not by broadcasting.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
question: Which handover note is most useful to the next shift?
options: "Quiet night, a few alerts, all handled"
A list of every alert ID closed during the shift
"C-311: waiting on user reply since 05:40; if none by 09:00, revoke sessions. Proxy logs silent since 02:00, ticket P-88"
"Ask me if anything comes up"
explain: The next shift needs open items, what each is blocked on, the next step with a deadline, and environmental changes such as a dead log source. A list of closed IDs or a vague summary gives them nothing to act on, and the author may be asleep.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
question: Which single field most changes the urgency of a push-storm alert?
options: Whether a push was approved after the storm
The number of pushes
The user's department
The phone's operating system
explain: Many denied pushes mean the attacker has the password but not the account yet: urgent, but contained (reset the password). An approval after a storm means the attacker may already hold a session, so revoke it now and find out what it did.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
question: At 02:14 a shadow-copy deletion alert fires on a file server. No other alerts yet. The on-call IR lead is asleep. What is the best first move?
options: Wait until the morning shift and investigate then
Restore the shadow copies
Email the server owner and wait for a reply
Page the IR lead now, isolate the host if the playbook pre-authorises it, and start collecting the process tree and the account that ran the command
explain: Recovery tampering is a late-stage precursor, and encryption may be minutes away. Paging at 02:14 is exactly what on-call exists for. Pre-authorised isolation buys time; evidence about the process and account tells IR how far the intrusion has spread.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: SOAR playbooks: what to automate and what to keep human
question: Which step is the best candidate for full automation with no human approval?
options: Disabling the CEO's account on a push-storm alert
Isolating a production database server on an EDR alert
Adding identity, asset owner and past-alert context to every new identity alert
Closing alerts whose destination IP has a benign reputation
explain: Enrichment is repetitive, fast and harmless if it errs: it only adds context for a human. The others are high-impact (CEO account, production database) or rely on reputation data that is easily wrong (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
question: Chrome's 2013 SSL warning had 70.2% clickthrough while its malware warning had 23.2%. What does Akhawe and Felt's comparison mostly show?
options: Chrome users are more reckless than Firefox users
The presentation and context of a warning strongly change behaviour
SSL errors are always harmless
Malware warnings are shown less often
explain: Chrome users heeded most malware warnings, and Firefox users heeded most SSL warnings. The large difference for one warning type in one browser points at that warning's design and context, not at the users.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing
question: Why is a video call that the requester arranges weak evidence of identity, even if the faces look right?
options: Because the requester controls that channel, so its content can be fabricated end to end
Because video calls are always encrypted
Because faces cannot be seen clearly on video
Because video calls are not recorded
explain: In the Arup case every participant except the victim was generated. Evidence produced inside a channel the attacker set up proves nothing about identity; only an independent channel does.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules
question: A company removes the bushes outside its ground-floor windows and lights the car park. Which CPTED approach is that?
options: Territorial behaviour
Natural access control
Natural surveillance
Target hardening with locks
explain: Clearing sightlines and adding light lets people see and be seen, which is natural surveillance. Access control steers movement; territorial behaviour marks ownership.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
question: A phishing simulation's click rate falls from 12% to 6%, and its report rate falls from 40% to 15%. Which reading is best?
options: The programme is working, since fewer people click
Reporting has collapsed, which removes the early warning the SOC depends on; investigate why
Click rate is the only metric that matters
The lure was too easy
explain: Fewer clicks with far fewer reports can mean people ignore or delete suspicious mail out of fear or fatigue. The report is what lets responders contain a real campaign.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: You train an SAE on layer 6 residual-stream activations of your GPT. Which statement is true?
options: The GPT's weights are updated so its neurons become monosemantic
The SAE has fewer hidden units than d_model so it compresses the activations
The SAE is trained on next-token cross-entropy only
The GPT is frozen; the SAE learns a wider, sparse re-description of the saved layer 6 vectors
explain: The SAE is a separate model trained on stored activations. It is overcomplete (M much larger than d) and trained with a reconstruction plus sparsity objective, not by changing the language model.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
question: Two SAEs on the same residual-stream layer: A has L0 = 40 and FVU = 0.30; B has L0 = 400 and FVU = 0.10. Which conclusion is justified from these numbers alone?
options: Neither dominates; compare them on the same L0 or the same FVU, and check delta LM loss
B is strictly better because its FVU is lower
A is strictly better because it is sparser
They must have the same downstream loss because they share a layer
explain: SAEs live on a sparsity versus fidelity frontier. B buys lower error with ten times more active latents. Fair comparisons hold one axis fixed, and downstream loss can rank SAEs differently from MSE.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Inverse distance weighting: weights from distance alone
question: You switch an IDW map from p = 1 to p = 6. What happens to the map?
options: It approaches nearest neighbor: flat patches around each sensor with sharper transitions between them
It becomes smoother everywhere
It starts extrapolating trends beyond the readings
Nothing, because weights are normalized
explain: A large power makes the nearest sensor dominate, so the map looks like Voronoi tiles with steeper transitions. Normalization keeps weights summing to 1, but it does not undo the change in their ratios.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
question: Why can the target model score 5 guessed tokens in roughly the time it takes to generate 1 token at batch size 1?
options: The target skips attention for guessed tokens
Guessed tokens use a lower precision path
The GPU runs 5 separate copies of the model in parallel
At small batch the step is memory bound: weights and KV cache are read once either way, and 5 token vectors add little arithmetic
explain: The cost of a small-batch decode step is dominated by reading weights and KV cache from memory. Multiplying those weights by 5 vectors instead of 1 adds arithmetic the chip has to spare, so latency barely changes (Chen et al.'s argument for linear layers, attention and all-reduces).

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
question: With s1 = 3, s2 = 2, s3 = 2, how many tree nodes must the target verify in one pass?
explain: Level sizes are 3, 3 x 2 = 6 and 3 x 2 x 2 = 12, for 3 + 6 + 12 = 21 nodes. Twelve full candidate paths share their prefixes, which is why tree attention is cheaper than 12 separate sequences of length 3.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: CTC and wav2vec 2.0: training without frame-level alignments
question: A CTC model must output the word too. Which frame path collapses to too?
options: t o o
t t o o o
t o _ o
_ t o o _
explain: Merging repeats turns t o o, t t o o o and _ t o o _ into to (or _to_, then to). Only t o _ o keeps two separate o runs, because the blank breaks the run before merging. Removing the blank then gives too.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
question: On 64-bit glibc, how many heap bytes does `malloc(25)` consume?
explain: request2size computes (25 + 8 + 15) rounded down to a multiple of 16 = 48. The 8-byte header pushes 25 bytes past the 32-byte minimum chunk, whose usable size is only 24.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
question: A process maps a 2 GiB file with `MAP_PRIVATE`, writes to 10 of its pages, and exits. What happened to the file on disk?
options: The 10 modified pages were written back at exit
Nothing: private mappings are copy-on-write, so the stores went to private copies
The whole file was rewritten
The write faulted with SIGSEGV because file mappings are read-only
explain: MAP_PRIVATE creates a private copy-on-write mapping: the first store to each page copies it, and updates are not carried through to the file. Only MAP_SHARED stores reach the page cache page and, through write-back, the file.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Directional ablation: what erasing the refusal direction reveals
question: Arditi et al. compared two ways of removing the refusal direction. Option A subtracts the refusal vector (x minus r) at one layer. Option B ablates r-hat at every layer. Both bypassed refusal comparably. What is B's advantage on harmless prompts?
options: B is faster at inference
B also improves MMLU (a multiple-choice knowledge benchmark, lesson 5)
A shifts every activation by a fixed amount, pushing harmless ones far past zero; B only removes what is there, so it raised loss on harmless data less
There is no difference on harmless prompts
explain: Subtraction moves all activations by the same vector, so prompts with little refusal content end up strongly negative along r, an unnatural state. Ablation sets the component to zero regardless. In the paper's comparison, activation addition in the negative direction caused higher loss on harmless data than directional ablation.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Beyond one fixed vector: conditional, learned and monitoring uses
question: You want a coding assistant to refuse only questions about medical diagnosis and answer everything else normally. Which approach fits best?
options: CAST: a medical-diagnosis condition vector gates a refusal behavior vector
Add a refusal vector at every forward pass with a small coefficient
Ablate the refusal direction at every layer
LEACE on the refusal concept
explain: A fixed vector shifts every prompt, so a small one is too weak on medical prompts and still leaks into others. Ablation and LEACE remove refusal rather than adding it selectively. CAST checks the hidden state against a condition direction and applies the refusal vector only when the condition fires.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
question: A Flink job reads a Kafka topic with 8 partitions. One partition stops receiving data. Per-minute windows stop producing results for all sensors. Why?
options: Kafka blocks all partitions when one is empty
Allowed lateness is too large
Tumbling windows require data in every partition
The operator's watermark is the minimum over its inputs, and the idle partition's watermark never advances
explain: Watermarks are tracked per partition and combined with a minimum. A silent partition pins the minimum, so no window end is ever passed. Marking idle inputs (withIdleness) lets the watermark advance without them.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
question: In the toy example, which statement about the attention weights of sat is correct?
options: sat attends most to itself because a token always matches its own key best
sat attends most to cat because q_sat dotted with k_cat = 2 is the largest score in its row
All four weights are equal because the values are different sizes
The weights depend on the value vectors
explain: Weights come only from query-key dot products: sat's row is (-1, 2, 1, 0) and the 2 belongs to cat. A token does not automatically match itself best, because W^Q and W^K are different matrices. Values only enter after the weights are fixed.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Relative positions: from sinusoids to RoPE and ALiBi
question: An ALiBi model has a head with slope 1/2 and a head with slope 1/256. Which one can still give a key 20 tokens back a weight comparable to the current token?
options: The slope-1/2 head, because steeper slopes reach further
Both equally, because the bias is the same for every head
Neither, because ALiBi masks keys more than 16 tokens back
The slope-1/256 head: its penalty at distance 20 is only about -0.08, against -10 for the other
explain: The penalty is slope times distance: 20 x 1/2 = 10 subtracted from the score, which shrinks that key's weight by a factor of e to the 10th (about 22,000), versus 20/256 = 0.078 for the shallow head. ALiBi biases scores; it does not mask distant keys.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
question: With k1 = 1.2 and average-length documents, doc P contains a term 2 times and doc Q contains it 20 times. Roughly how much larger is Q's factor than P's?
options: About 1.5 times larger (0.94 vs 0.62)
10 times larger
Exactly the same
About 3 times larger
explain: P: 2/(2+1.2) = 0.625. Q: 20/(21.2) = 0.943. The ratio is about 1.5, not 10. That is saturation: ten times the count gives about one and a half times the weight.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
question: A bug report: the mask was built with `torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T))` instead of `torch.tril(...)`, keeping the `masked_fill(mask == 0, -inf)` line unchanged. What does position 0 attend to now?
options: Only itself, as before
All positions 0 to T-1, including the future
Nothing, so its row is all minus infinity
Only position T-1
explain: triu keeps the upper triangle, so row 0 keeps columns 0 to T-1 and the model sees the whole future from the first position. The last row is the one that keeps just one key, its own. The loss will look great and generation will fail.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: You delete the line `loss = loss / grad_accum_steps` from a GPT run that uses AdamW and clips the gradient norm at 1.0. What changes?
options: The effective learning rate becomes grad_accum_steps times larger and the run diverges
The gradients become grad_accum_steps times smaller
The updates barely change, since Adam divides by the gradient's running scale, but the gradient norm is now grad_accum_steps times too big, so clipping fires on almost every step
Nothing at all, because each micro-batch loss is already a mean
explain: We tried it on a 2-layer character GPT with 8 micro-steps for 200 AdamW steps: validation loss 2.398 with or without the division, but clipping fired on all 200 steps instead of 51. With plain SGD (lr 0.5, no clipping) the same mistake diverged to NaN. The prerequisite course's rule (learning rate times the number of micro-steps) is the SGD story; with Adam the main damage is a clip threshold that no longer means what you set.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
question: At one step your model's distribution is very flat (hundreds of plausible tokens); at another it is very peaked (one token at 95%). Which setting adapts the candidate set to both?
options: Top-k with k = 40
Greedy decoding
Temperature 1.5
Top-p with p = 0.9
explain: Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching 90% of the mass: just one token when it alone holds 95%, hundreds when the distribution is flat. A fixed k = 40 is too many for the peaked case and may cut plausible options in the flat one; greedy ignores diversity; temperature reshapes but does not truncate.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: The multivariable chain rule: summing over every path
question: In a network, one hidden value $h$ feeds two later layers. Backprop delivers $\partial L/\partial h = 0.3$ from the first and $-0.5$ from the second. What gradient should $h$ pass further back?
options: 0.3, the first one to arrive
-0.5, the last one to arrive
-0.1, their average
-0.2, their sum
explain: The loss depends on $h$ through both layers, so the multivariable chain rule adds the two contributions: $0.3 + (-0.5) = -0.2$. Keeping only the first or last is the overwrite bug; averaging has no basis in the chain rule.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
question: A directory has mode 750 (`rwxr-x---`). You are not its owner but you are in its group. What can you do?
options: List, enter and create files in it
List it and enter it, but not create or delete files in it
Nothing, because only the owner has rwx
Enter it but not list it
explain: The group digit 5 is r-x: r lets you list the names and x lets you enter and reach files inside. Creating or deleting entries needs w on the directory, which the group lacks. Others (digit 0) get nothing at all.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
question: You want to keep only the errors of `make` in `errors.txt` and still see normal output on the terminal. Which works?
options: `make > errors.txt`
`make 2>&1 > errors.txt`
`make 2> errors.txt`
`make > errors.txt 2>&1`
explain: `2>` redirects fd 2 alone. The first option captures normal output instead, the last captures both, and `2>&1 > errors.txt` leaves errors on the terminal and puts normal output in the file, the opposite of what you want.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
question: You press Ctrl-Z while a long `make` runs, then type `ls`. What state is make in, and how do you let it continue while keeping your prompt?
options: It was killed; rerun it as `make &`
It keeps running in the background already, so nothing is needed
It is stopped; `bg` resumes it in the background
It is stopped; `fg` resumes it and keeps the prompt free
explain: Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, which stops the process without ending it. `bg` sends SIGCONT and lets it run in the background while you keep the prompt. `fg` would also resume it, but in the foreground, taking the terminal back.
